near_miss.lead: Water pouring and naming; ausa vatni versus ἀφυσσάμεθ̓ ὕδωρ
near_miss.why_not: The Norse infinitive ausa governs instrumental/dative vatni in infant sprinkling and naming; Homer has middle aorist plus accusative water in drawing supplies after landing. Searches of the water and drawing roots confirm repeated Norse naming formulas, but Greek water drawing and wine scooping, not matching infant ritual. Irish water and names in these bundles belong to different clauses or a stream naming narrative. Cognate verb and liquid are real, but the ritual, valency and discourse function do not establish inherited wording.

near_miss.lead: Hearing words: heyra orð and Greek hearing speech
near_miss.why_not: Close reading gives a commonplace request to hear a king, compared with a procedural discussion of persuasive speeches. Greek ῥήσει is instrumental rather than the object of hearing, and is not the same etymon as orð. Searching ἀκούω with ῥῆμα produced ordinary speech and hearing across several prose genres, without the distinctive framing needed to posit an inherited formula.

near_miss.lead: Night and seeing in sleep: nóttina, i svefni, sa; nocte, in somnis
near_miss.why_not: The night and sleep nouns are cognate, and the Norse and Plautine scenes both involve a supernatural dream visitor. Their seeing verbs are not cognate, however, and night is a temporal adjunct independent of the sleep expression. Searches found ordinary Norse sleep constructions and Greek night/sleep combinations in military and medical prose. These everyday circumstances do not establish a formula. The Norse passage is a Christian saint miracle, further weakening inference of independent inherited ritual diction.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_1_06_Yeghishe ed. page 579 - PDF page 59 (word id 9376)
near_miss.lead: Father, mother and other kin as a possible family merism
near_miss.why_not: The Irish welcomes explicitly coordinate father and mother; the Norse pivots chain genealogical dependencies, including mother of one person and father of another. In bundle BS-e1b1f, Sanskrit absence of protectors, Irish identity/relinquishment and Armenian polemic enumerate different relatives in different relations. The shared kin nouns do not preserve one distinctive syntactic figure or context.

near_miss.lead: Weapons sticking: festi a honom versus ἐν χροῒ πήγνυτ / πῆχθεν
near_miss.why_not: Norse denies weapon penetration because of magic, while Homer says missiles lodged in flesh. The apparent fastening-root correspondence is only one lexical element; Norse has a personal pronoun where Homer names skin, and vápn is not cognate with the Greek weapon nouns in context. Searching πήγνυμι shows the same verb with ground, shields, belly, heart and ships. This is ordinary fastening/penetration vocabulary, insufficient for inherited phraseology.

near_miss.lead: Great deeds: Stór verc and μέγα ἔργον
near_miss.why_not: The nouns are cognate but the adjectives are not. Norse celebrates exploits; Thucydides evaluates the magnitude of an additional military undertaking. Generic adjective-plus-work syntax with this semantic difference supplies no distinctive inherited phrase.

Norse rejects a higher royal title. A nomen/fero search found Lucretius 6.372, nomine ... fertur, describing the season called autumn. The Latin passive with ablative of designation is not the Norse active verb with accusative title. This ordinary naming metaphor is not sufficient evidence for an inherited collocation; the slab partners supply none.

near_miss.lead: Warm blood entering the sea; bloð ... varmt
near_miss.why_not: No cross-branch slab partner reproduces the blood and warmth collocation: the Irish material concerns poets or martial prowess, the Welsh grief and a heart breaking. A Greek parallel found by searching is recorded separately as a search lead; it cannot supply the missing second slab anchor.

search_lead.cognate: Norse varmt (neuter singular of varmr, agreeing with blóð) and Greek θερμόν (neuter singular of θερμός, agreeing with αἷμα) continue the warmth root *gʷʰer-. The blood nouns and motion verbs are not cognate.
search_lead.argument: Both poetic battle scenes specify warm blood in motion: the Norse blood comes into the sea, while Homer describes blood still welling from a wound. This is a candidate for an inherited epithet with lexical renewal of the blood noun, but warmth is a natural property of freshly shed blood, and the shared adjective alone cannot distinguish inheritance from independent description. Submitted for wider comparison, not as a claim.

error.evidence: The subject is Ragnhilldr dróttning and the object son; the following child is sprinkled and named Haraldr. The ale etymon is inapplicable.
